tagline: Along Bayou Lafourche, roads follow the water toward a barrier island.
intro: Highway 1 follows the west bank of Bayou Lafourche, with Highway 308 across the water on the east. At Larose, the bayou intersects the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway; farther south, the drive reaches Grand Isle, a barrier island at the mouth of Barataria Bay.

Water transport shaped the towns before the highway took its present course. At Lockport, a canal intended to connect Bayou Terrebonne with New Orleans opened in 1847, followed three years later by locks at Bayou Lafourche. The bayou itself changed in 1904, when a dam severed its natural connection to the Mississippi River. A pumping station began supplying water in 1950.

Follow the bayou from Lockport to Larose, then continue south through Galliano toward Golden Meadow. At Leeville, Highway 1 crosses Bayou Lafourche on the Gateway to the Gulf Expressway. The road reaches Grand Isle by its western causeway and becomes the town’s main street, with marsh, beaches and hardwood chenier forests on the island.

moments.title: Lockport
moments.text: Lockport’s name belongs to an ambitious canal connection. William Field donated land on both banks of Bayou Lafourche to the Barataria and Lafourche Canal Company, which agreed to connect Bayou Terrebonne with New Orleans. The canal opened in 1847 and its locks followed in 1850. Shipping stayed brisk until 1868; afterward, part of the waterway fell out of use. A crevasse partially destroyed the locks in 1876, leaving brick bulwark remnants that remain visible beneath weeds. Later, Highway 1 moved off Main Street, and businesses along its new route became the town’s commercial center.

moments.title: Leeville
moments.text: Survivors of the Chenier Caminada Hurricane founded this community in November 1893. First called Orange City, it was renamed for Pierre Charles Lee and his wife, Rosalie Albarado. By 1938, Leeville had 297 producing oil wells. Studies by the Barataria-Terrebonne National Estuary Program found that around 70 percent of the surrounding wetlands had vanished since 1932.

moments.title: Grand Isle
moments.text: The highway arrives on a barrier island where hardwood trees grow on slightly elevated ridges. These chenier forests provide resting places for birds before or after their flight across the Gulf of Mexico. The ridges formed as sediment accumulated during shifts of the Mississippi River’s delta. That small difference in elevation also helps the forests act as a barrier to saltwater intrusion into marshes during storm surges. Grand Isle State Park occupies the island’s eastern tip. Oaks and hackberries are the principal trees in these forests, which occupy higher ground within a landscape of marsh and beach.
